properties.history: Begun in 1873 about two miles southwest of Mount Carmel to work the Mammoth Vein, the Alaska shaft shipped 2,510 tons on its first day in 1874, the same year (March 15) a fire destroyed its unfinished engine, boiler and shaft houses. The coal shaft went down 99 yards (about 300 feet) to the Mammoth, which lay 20 feet thick there and dipped 10 degrees south. It had two hoisting compartments, a pump way and an air way. An air shaft (52 yards) followed in 1875, with a powerful Guibal fan; in 1878 the state inspector named Alaska one of the best-ventilated collieries in his district. In the inspectors' reports from 1876 to 1887 it usually appears as the "Mount Carmel Shaft" (in 1878, "near Alaska station, between Locust Gap and borough of Mount Carmel"), which is why deaths there in those years were long missing from Alaska's record. The colliery stood at Alaska Junction (Alaska station) on the Shamokin & Mount Carmel Railroad. On June 5, 1886, the breaker burned along with an adjoining sawmill; at full capacity it had handled about 25,000 tons a month with 500 workers. In 1889 a hoisting slope was sunk from the main west gangway 183 yards into the basin to raise output, and in 1890 a 12-foot fan was put on the Skidmore vein. In June 1897 the Baldwin Locomotive Works supplied a compound compressed-air locomotive for underground haulage. By 1899 Alaska was the Reading Company's largest operation in the region, employing nearly 1,000 men and boys; that year a tunnel was driven toward the Lykens Valley Vein, which was not found in workable condition. Annie Oakley and her company toured the underground workings and the breaker in November 1902. In 1904 a No. 3 slope was being sunk in the bottom bench of the Mammoth. In 1913 the company set out to make Alaska the largest electrically operated mine in the anthracite fields, and by 1915 it had mechanical loading and electric haulage. It employed 777 people in 1920. On April 19, 1926, a fire that began in the conveyor line destroyed the uninsured wooden breaker, about $500,000 in damage, idling some 650 men underground. Rising pumping costs led the company to announce an abandonment plan in April 1944; in September 1950 the UMWA's Alaska local campaigned to keep it open with a new slope to the Lykens Vein, with about 500 jobs at stake. P.&R. C.&I. closed the colliery on April 30, 1954, with about 300 men still employed, saying its profitable reserves were exhausted. The Reading Anthracite Company then strip-mined the site, demolishing the colliery and the century-old village of Alaska (about 40 residents in 1958).

properties.history: The Susquehanna Coal Company, a Pennsylvania Railroad subsidiary, reached the site in 1894 with the 2.95-mile Scott Branch of the Shamokin Valley and Pottsville Railroad. The Union Coal Company had begun sinking two shafts in 1893 (the first, with four hoisting compartments, was 100 feet down by year's end), but the 1894 slump stopped the work and the shafts filled with water. The main hoisting shaft was completed in 1898 by African American workers whose families settled in company homes at the end of Poplar Street, the first residential community in what became Kulpmont. The colliery stood idle and flooded again in 1903. In 1904 a new breaker of Georgia long-leaf yellow pine on concrete foundations was going up, with 1,500 horsepower of boilers. Immigrant families followed in a 1905 building boom, and Kulpmont incorporated as a borough in 1915. In 1913 a concrete-block wash-house for the miners opened, with lockers and hot and cold showers, and in 1914 a new fan was installed on an air shaft at the anticline that divided the Scott and Hickory Ridge workings. Ownership passed to the Susquehanna Collieries Company in 1917, which electrified its mines by 1922, the same year the M.A. Hanna Company bought it out. The colliery closed in 1928. Its culm bank, south of the borough, caught fire in the years after the closing, but in 1975 it was still standing, its fire almost entirely burned out. The flooded workings still drain through the Scott Ridge Mine Tunnel into Shamokin Creek.

properties.history: Named for Lehigh Valley Railroad vice president and chief engineer Robert H. Sayre, the colliery was developed by the Lehigh Valley Coal Company to replace the neighboring Mount Carmel (Stuartville) Colliery, which was abandoned in 1905. A deep vertical shaft sunk north of the old workings opened new sections of the Mammoth Vein, and the Lehigh Valley Railroad carried its coal to eastern markets. In 1906 the state inspector reported that the new Sayre breaker could prepare 1,800 tons in a nine-hour day, using 32 Lehigh Valley jigs. In 1913 the company ran a power line from Sayre to the Sioux No. 3 slope to drive its underground haulage, and in 1917 it finished a tunnel from the north-dip Mammoth to the south-dip Skidmore vein to mine the Skidmore under old Stuartsville. Deep mining ended around 1930, when the company shut its Western Middle Field operations as Depression-era prices fell and pumping costs mounted. In the 1960s Robert Kerris Sr. and Ed Helfrick acquired the property for strip mining. Parts of the land later became the Den-Mar Gardens neighborhood and commercial sites along Route 61.

properties.history: Thos. Baumgardner & Co. sank the Reliance shaft on Locust Mountain south of Mount Carmel and shipped its first coal on January 16, 1867. In 1871 the state inspector listed the Locust Mountain Coal Company as operator, working a drift and a slope on the Mammoth (E) vein with 150 hands; Baumgardner & Co. ran it under lease from the Philadelphia & Reading by 1873. By 1874 the double-track slope reached 370 yards down the north dip of the Mammoth at 17 degrees, and in 1889 it was extended to the fourth level, 413 yards from the top. A 12-foot Guibal fan and new cast-iron slate-picking tables came in 1884. The Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company had taken control by 1902, when it brought in armed deputies to guard the colliery during the anthracite strike. In 1896 Reliance shipped 134,216 tons and employed 436 men. A gas explosion at the Beaverdale Shaft on September 2, 1926, set off when a smoker lit a match in a gassy section, burned eight miners; Lawrence Fracalossi, Michael Rice, Stephen Homiak and John Boriak died. The workforce was 685 in April 1940 and still over 400 in 1950. From 1930 a cleaner plant at Reliance sent raw coal to the company's new Locust Summit Central Breaker. The mines feeding Locust Summit were put on standby in January 1955. The Reading Anthracite Company then strip-mined the site as the Reliance Pit, and its expansion in 1958 destroyed the neighboring village of Alaska.

properties.status: Breaker razed (1986 per one source, 2000 per another — unresolved); large culm bank remains along PA Route 61, leased to Reading Anthracite Co. for reprocessing
properties.history: Worked from the late 1830s as small drift mines known as the Gap, the site passed to William Cameron in 1841 and was formally renamed the Cameron Colliery in the 1860s. In 1870 the state inspector described Haas, Fagely & Co.'s Cameron colliery, a mile west of Shamokin on the Cameron, Packer & Co. estate, as four drifts above water level; by 1873 the Mineral Railroad & Mining Company was operating it with five drifts and a new double-track slope. A slope on the Lykens Valley vein followed in 1876, and by 1880 the No. 2 slope was 250 yards deep on a 40-degree pitch. The mine was gassy: four gas explosions in 1881 burned eight men, and in 1881–82 the inspector had workers prosecuted for riding loaded cars up the slopes; Northumberland County juries convicted them. A new shaft was sunk in 1895 to reach unmined ground, and on February 28, 1904, a fire that started in the pump house had to be fought underground. The Pennsylvania Railroad's Mineral Railroad & Mining Company ran it through the turn of the century, building a 224-locker bathhouse in 1912. Ownership passed to the Susquehanna Coal Company and then, in 1917, to the Susquehanna Collieries Company. Leased to the Stevens Coal Company in the 1930s, which built a new breaker in 1937, the mine returned to Susquehanna control in March 1940 and was renamed Glen Burn. Production peaked in 1942 at 627,158 tons. Kerris & Helfrick Inc. bought the property in 1966 and ran a public mine tour from 1968 to 1977. Deep mining ended in 1970. A later small independent operation is reported to have worked the site from the late 1980s to about 1995, though this is unconfirmed. The colliery's large refuse bank, long a local landmark, still stands beside Route 61.

properties.status: Pumping suspended and colliery abandoned, January 1934; flooded
properties.history: Opened by Jacob Mowry in 1837 on the Mammoth Vein, the colliery passed through several lessees before Bird, Douty & John took it over around 1856 — independently confirmed by Bell's 1891 county history, which records John Blundin Douty leasing the "Big Mountain colliery" around October 1856. J. Langdon & Co. worked the Buck Ridge side from 1867 and opened the Mahanoy Drifts in 1869. In 1870 the inspector listed "J. Langdon Heirs' Big Mountain colliery," a mile and a half south of Shamokin, as five water-level drifts on the Twin (Mammoth) veins. Patterson, Llewellyn & Co. operated it from 1873, sinking a 143-yard double-track slope on the No. 8 vein in 1881 and installing a 16-foot fan; a second hoisting slope (No. 2) was sunk in 1889. The Philadelphia & Reading Coal and Iron Company took over in 1886 and ran it thereafter as a section of the Henry Clay Colliery, sinking a new slope in 1903 and driving a tunnel to the Lykens Valley vein in 1919. Reading suspended pumping and abandoned the mine in January 1934, letting it flood. Total shipments reached 2,442,806 tons by 1886; later output was counted together with the Henry Clay Colliery and not reported separately. Its shaft pump was still in service as of 1933–1935, handling drainage water diverted from the nearby, by-then-closed Burnside Colliery.

properties.status: Abandoned by Philadelphia & Reading shortly after a May 31, 1889 gas explosion; site later used as a smallpox isolation center around the turn of the century; the Greenback Patch community has entirely disappeared
properties.history: Greenback Colliery and its "mine patch" were built in the early 1870s, two and a half miles east of Shamokin, and named after the Greenback Party, then a rising political movement — confirming the colliery's existence by 1871, when it also appears (as "Greenbaok," an OCR misreading) in the index of the Pennsylvania mine inspector's Third (Shamokin) District annual report. The inspector's reports suggest the mine itself is older than that: in 1870 the Greenback colliery, on the Brady Coal Company estate three miles east of Shamokin, was described as four years in operation, with a slope 65 yards deep on the Mammoth vein pitching 47 degrees; Colter & Gorman were the operators in 1871. In 1882 the slope was sunk another 73-yard lift and tunnels were driven south to the Skidmore and Buck Mountain veins, and a 12-foot fan and a 60-horsepower hoisting engine followed. A fire in the No. 9 vein water-level gangway in 1890 was put out by turning water into the mine for several days. In size it compared with the Benjamin Franklin, Buck Ridge, and Garfield collieries. It was considered hazardous from the start because of free gas, with frequent gas explosions caused by open-flame lighting. Early settlers were German Catholics who later resettled in Shamokin; in the late 1880s some of the area's first Ukrainian immigrants settled there instead. At its height the patch held about 10 two-family wooden-frame homes and a public school (no churches; union religious services were held in the schoolhouse), and two passenger trains stopped there daily besides the local miners' trains. The Philadelphia & Reading Coal and Iron Company had purchased the colliery shortly before August 21, 1884, when a gas explosion/asphyxiation disaster killed eight men while crews worked to flood the adjoining, burning Buck Ridge mine — the two collieries' underground workings connected. On May 31, 1889, the day of the Johnstown Flood, a second gas explosion in the Greenback Slope injured 22 men; Philadelphia & Reading abandoned the Greenback mine shortly afterward, around 1889. The same account states Buck Ridge Colliery was abandoned at the same time, for the same reason — see the note on Buck Ridge's entry, since this conflicts with another source's claim of a c. 1900 Buck Ridge abandonment. The miners who lost work slowly moved elsewhere, and the patch was later used as an isolation center during a smallpox epidemic around the turn of the century. Nothing of Greenback remains today.
properties.confidence: Medium. The 1884 disaster is well-documented (contemporary NYT report + state annual report). The 1871 existence is a bare index listing. The rest — founding date, naming, demographics, the 1889 explosion and abandonment, and the smallpox-isolation use — comes from a single reader-submitted reminiscence published decades after the fact in a local-history newspaper column. It's detailed and specific (a dated event, a named contributor), which is worth more than an anonymous claim, but it is still one uncorroborated secondary account, not a contemporary record. Treat the 1889 closure as credible but not certain.

properties.history: Opened in 1863 by Stephen Bittenbender Son & Co. with a drift on the Topsput Mammoth Vein, first shipping 20,257 tons in 1864. Isaac May & Co. took over in 1871 and sank slopes on the Holmes and South Dip Top Split Mammoth veins. In 1870 the state inspector described it as a single slope 80 feet deep on the Mammoth vein, on the Big Mountain Improvement Company estate about 2½ miles south of Shamokin; by 1875, under May, Morgan & Co., it worked a double-track slope on the nine-foot vein, ventilated by a 20-horsepower fan. The Philadelphia & Reading Coal and Iron Company took possession in 1878, working two slopes on the north and south dips of the No. 9 (Twin) vein at Carbon Run, and developed it for large-scale production, sinking the main shaft on the Skidmore Vein in 1897 to a third level at 724 feet. The breaker was entirely remodeled in 1910, and in 1915 a concrete-and-brick miners' wash-house with shower baths and lockers was built. Total shipments reached 12,965,738 tons by 1928. Pumping was suspended March 26, 1933, and the colliery abandoned; a drainage tunnel kept its water from reaching the adjoining Sterling Colliery, and from July 1933 to January 1935 that water was diverted to the Big Mountain Colliery's shaft pump before a brick dam sealed the tunnel.

The Philadelphia & Reading Coal and Iron Company took control in 1885, and on November 22, 1886 started operations at a newly rebuilt, massive Henry Clay breaker that processed coal from the Big Mountain, Peerless, and Sterling mines, with a capacity of about 1,500 wagons (300 carloads) per day; coal from the Big Mountain mine was hauled in by small locomotives pulling 20-wagon trains, making 20–25 trips daily. To power it, the company put up twelve large boilers in 1890 and twenty-four more in 1891. At 7:30 a.m. on October 11, 1894, 27 of the 34 boilers exploded for no reason anyone could find, wrecking the boiler house, throwing a boiler through the breaker and killing seven men and boys; 1,600 employees were idled until the plant was rebuilt. A new air shaft with a 12-foot fan followed in 1895. The breaker operated until 1932. Mine pumping was stopped and the colliery abandoned in November 1933, and the breaker itself was dismantled in 1939.

The 1890 state mine inspector's report listed Righter, Leisenring & Co. as operator, and the colliery (sometimes spelled "Mid Valley," sometimes "Midvalley") was part of the Leisenring and Wentz family group of companies, later becoming the Mid Valley Coal Company. By 1891 the main slope was finished, and the company had built its own town for its workers, Wilburton, laid out on the mountaintop a quarter mile east of the breaker. The breaker burned in June 1893 and a replacement was in operation by that November. Shortly after 1900 the mine flooded and work stopped until a new pump house was built and the mine reopened. properties.history: The No. 1 shaft was sunk 1888-1890 to a depth of 754 feet, developed on both the north and south dips of the Maple Hill Basin; the colliery worked 17 veins ranging from the 12-foot Buck Mountain to the 43-foot Mammoth. The shaft stood between the Ellangowan and Suffolk collieries, and by 1893 the inspector called Maple Hill "a model anthracite colliery, both as regards inside and outside equipment," with a 21-foot fan over a new air shaft. In 1903 he described it as one of the Philadelphia & Reading's most modern and largest-producing collieries. First shipment, 113,887 tons, came in 1892, rising to 307,246 tons in 1893. Three air locomotives replaced mule haulage in 1901 (82 mules had handled all output before then). The No. 2 shaft, with six compartments (four for coal, two for water), was sunk to 1,050 feet in 1903, and an underground slope reached the same depth on the Buck Mountain vein by 1906. Wooden headframes were replaced with steel in 1911. Cumulative shipments reached 16,091,438 tons by 1928. By 1938 haulage included 19 air locomotives and 27 mules, with electrification of the haulage system beginning that year; the last eight mules were retired in September 1948. Cumulative shipments totaled 27,676,556 tons by January 1, 1949. Mining ceased June 25, 1955.
properties.confidence: Good for dates (precise opening development 1888-1890 and exact closing date June 25, 1955), though sourced to a single detailed secondary source not yet independently cross-checked. Coordinates supplied by Tom.

properties.status: Closed 1962 when Coates Coal Co. ended operations; a small amount of coal was remined from the culm dump by George Racho in 1960 and processed at the Diamond Breaker. This colliery is unrelated to the Centralia mine fire, which began in 1962 at the borough's landfill/strip-mine pit, not at this colliery.
properties.history: Sources differ on the exact opening date, placing it between 1857 and 1862; the state mine inspector wrote in 1871 that it had been working "some 14 years." Early operator Joseph M. Freck worked it through a slope on the south dip of the Mammoth (E) vein, on the Locust Mountain Coal & Iron Company estate; the slope was 220 yards deep in 1870 and 320 yards in two lifts by 1871. The breaker burned in 1870 and was rebuilt. In the early 1870s the mine flooded; Dr. G.M. Provost pumped it out, opened a new slope on the Skidmore vein in 1876, and was in full production by 1878. Lewis A. Reilly & Co. operated it from 1880 to the mid-1890s (the partnership is recorded in 1880–81 as Reilly, Lilley & Lentz), after which the Lehigh Valley Coal Co. mined it both underground and by stripping into the early 1930s. In 1896, two boiler explosions killed six men: one on the night of February 24–25 and one at 5:30 a.m. on November 7, when a boiler was hurled 500 yards and bricks rained on the houses of Frick's village by the breaker. Under the Lehigh Valley, the neighboring Continental shaft was deepened (1903), and in 1913 a central power plant was built at Centralia, with a transmission line to Continental. The Centralia Collieries Co. revived the mine in 1935, followed by the Mahanoy Coal Mining Co. during World War II and the Centralia Mining Co. afterward, which deep-mined, strip-mined, and remined culm banks. The C.Q. & W. Coal Co. mined there in 1949, and the Coates Coal Co. leased the property in 1955, ending operations in 1962. In 1960 George Racho remined a small amount of coal from the culm dump, processed at the Diamond Breaker.
properties.confidence: Medium-good for the operator chain and 1962 closing date, from one detailed secondary source not yet independently cross-checked; opening date is explicitly uncertain even within that source (1857-1862 range). Coordinates supplied by Tom. Note: this historic colliery is a separate thing from the famous Centralia mine fire (which started in 1962 at a landfill/strip-mine pit, not here) — worth keeping distinct on the map to avoid confusing the two.

properties.history: J. Langdon & Co. opened Hickory Ridge around 1869, three and a half miles east of Shamokin on Northern Central Railway land, with two tunnels driven south into the coal. The Mineral Railroad & Mining Company, a Pennsylvania Railroad company, owned and ran it from 1873. Its breaker burned on the night of November 4, 1878, and a small new breaker replaced it; a new slope begun in 1881 was 400 feet deep by 1889. In 1907 the breaker was remodeled to prepare Hickory Swamp's coal as well, which a 16-ton locomotive hauled two miles over new track. Electric haulage came in 1914. To the south, an anticline in the No. 8 seam divided Hickory Ridge's workings from the Scott Colliery's. Like its neighbors it passed to the Susquehanna Coal Company and, in 1917, the Susquehanna Collieries Company; the state registers record deaths there until 1942.

properties.history: The Shamokin Coal Company was working Hickory Swamp in 1870, two and a half miles east of Shamokin on Northern Central Railway land along Coal Run, through a tunnel, two drifts and a slope on the Mammoth's twin veins; by 1871 the slope was 180 yards deep. The Mineral Railroad & Mining Company ran it from 1873, and the Union Coal Company by 1890. Its breaker was completely remodeled and enlarged in 1893, but from 1907 Hickory Swamp's coal went by locomotive to the Hickory Ridge breaker instead. Electric hoists, an aerial tramway for boiler ashes (1913) and a 379-foot No. 4 slope (by 1917) followed. The Susquehanna Collieries Company abandoned Hickory Swamp together with Luke Fidler in December 1928. Local miners reopened the Hickory Swamp Slope about 1935 and shipped its coal to the Pennsylvania Colliery; the state registers record deaths there into the 1950s.

properties.history: The Locust Gap colliery worked the steeply pitching Mammoth vein in the water gap where Locust Creek cuts through Locust Ridge, about six miles east of Shamokin. By the early 1870s the Philadelphia & Reading Coal & Iron Company was operating it with a double-track coal slope and a single-track pump slope on the Mammoth (E) vein. In 1899 a new breaker built at Locust Gap replaced both the Locust Gap and the neighboring Locust Spring breakers. The colliery worked through East, West and Buck Mountain slopes. At dawn on May 5, 1904, fire swept both slopes and the fan-way of Locust Gap East, burning down the fan and trapping five men: John J. Boylan, Michael Boylan, John Debo, William Meleschefskie and Michael Shannon. All five died. From 1930 its coal went to the new Locust Summit Central Breaker, and it worked on into the 1950s.

properties.history: William Montelius's Stewartsville colliery, at the east end of Mount Carmel on the Locust Mountain Coal & Iron Company estate, had been working about twelve years in 1870, through a slope down the south dip of the Mammoth vein. In 1879 a rock slope was driven through to the Skidmore vein, with a new air shaft, hoisting engines and a 12-foot fan. Its breaker burned and a new one was built in 1880. By 1891 it was working the Mammoth and Skidmore veins from a No. 5 slope, hauling the coal overland to the breaker. In 1904 the Lehigh Valley Coal Company began sinking the eight-compartment Sayre shaft just north of the colliery to replace it, and the old Mount Carmel colliery was abandoned in 1905. The ground was later strip-mined.

properties.history: Work on the Richards colliery began in July 1892 on the north edge of Mount Carmel, and it shipped its first coal in June 1893. Two slopes were sunk 810 feet (two lifts) on the lower split of the Mammoth vein, and a large breaker was built that superintendent John L. Williams expected to ship 2,000 tons a day. That same month, mine foreman Thomas Williams was killed by a car that ran down the slope as he was being lowered. In 1897 the inspector described the Union Coal Company's method of robbing pillars at Richards, which he reckoned would recover a million more tons of coal. In the 1902 anthracite strike, strikers attacked a train carrying non-union men to the Richards and Pennsylvania collieries, and the state sent troops. Under the Susquehanna companies the colliery added the Richards No. 4 mine, a concrete-block wash-house for the miners (1913), a long water-level tunnel and 150 steel cars (1914–15), and a shaft for rope haulage (1917). The state registers record deaths there until 1945.

properties.history: The Natalie colliery and its company village stood in the hills north-west of Mount Carmel, reached by the Mount Carmel & Natalie railroad. In February 1895, while a slope was being sunk, laborer Steve Barross was killed when a wagon ran down it after the safety blocks failed on a cold morning. In 1897 newspapers described the Natalie plant as worth about $2,000,000 and long tied up in litigation, with plans to put it back in operation. Company maps show the breaker beside the railroad at the west end of the village, with No. 1 slope and No. 1 Lykens slope nearby. In 1915 a new steel boiler house and a 7,500-foot water line were built. The state registers record deaths there until 1947.
